title: Vendor thread hijack
scenario: A familiar supplier email thread requests payment to a new bank account. The reply-to address differs slightly and the attached invoice has changed bank details.
options: Update the bank details because the thread is familiar.
Reply to the same email for confirmation.
Pause payment and call the supplier using a previously verified number; follow the bank-change approval process.
Ask another colleague to choose.
explanation: A compromised mailbox can continue a genuine thread. Independently verify payment changes using trusted contact details.

title: Microsoft 365 sign-in lure
scenario: An urgent email links to a Microsoft-looking page. The actual host is login.microsoftonline.com.verify365.co, not microsoftonline.com.
options: Open it in private browsing to check.
Do not open it; report it and navigate through a known company bookmark.
Reply to ask if it is genuine.
Open it but do not type your password.
explanation: The registered domain is verify365.co. A copied login design and HTTPS do not prove legitimacy.

title: Inspect the actual URL
scenario: HR displays benefits.fujisilvertech.com/renew, but inspection reveals https://fujisilvertech.com.attacker-example.net/renew.
options: Trust the visible text.
Click once and inspect the address bar.
Paste it into a search engine.
Do not follow it; inspect the destination, report the mismatch and use the known HR portal.
explanation: The true domain is attacker-example.net. Visible link text can differ from the underlying destination.

title: QR-code office poster
scenario: An unapproved poster asks staff to scan a QR code to refresh Wi-Fi access and sign in with company credentials.
options: Scan using a personal phone.
Verify with IT through a known channel, report the poster and use official Wi-Fi instructions.
Enter only your email.
Ask a colleague to scan first.
explanation: QR codes conceal destinations and physical placement does not establish legitimacy.

title: MFA fatigue and fake helpdesk
scenario: You receive repeated unexpected MFA prompts. A caller claiming to be IT asks you to approve one prompt to stop them.
options: Approve one while on the call.
Read the caller the code.
Deny prompts, end the call and contact IT through the published service-desk channel.
Disable MFA temporarily.
explanation: Unexpected prompts may indicate password compromise. Never approve an uninitiated request or share codes.

title: Targeted spear-phishing
scenario: A leader asks for a confidential project spreadsheet before a board meeting and says not to involve the project owner. The sender uses an external lookalike address.
options: Send a password-protected copy.
Verify through a known internal channel and report the suspicious sender.
Ask the sender to confirm the project code by email.
Upload it to a personal cloud drive.
explanation: Public company details make spear-phishing convincing. Secrecy, urgency and sensitive data require independent verification.

title: Supplier bank-detail change
scenario: A formal supplier letter requests a new bank account. Invoice and purchase order details match, and payment is due today.
options: Update the supplier record.
Reply to the same email for confirmation.
Hold the change and verify with an authorized supplier contact already on file, using dual approval.
Send a small test payment.
explanation: Matching invoice details and a signature image are not proof. Verify bank changes independently.

title: Executive gift-card request
scenario: A senior executive's display name asks you to buy gift cards and send redemption codes, claiming they cannot take calls.
options: Buy them and keep receipts.
Ask a coworker to buy them.
Send one code first.
Do not purchase or share codes; verify through a known executive channel and report the impersonation.
explanation: Gift-card codes are cash-equivalent. Urgency and inability to verify are common impersonation signals.

title: Tailgating and visitor pretext
scenario: A person carrying equipment says their badge is being reprinted and asks you to hold a secure door. They know a manager's name.
options: Let them in because they know a manager.
Direct them to reception/security; do not allow piggybacking.
Escort them into the office first.
Photograph their ID and let them enter.
explanation: Knowledge of staff names is easy to obtain. Visitors must follow check-in and escort procedures.

title: Payroll direct-deposit change
scenario: An email appearing to come from HR requests bank details and identity documents through an attached form before payroll closes.
options: Complete it because the deadline is close.
Reply with only the account number.
Ask a teammate if they received it.
Do not use the attachment; verify with HR through the official portal and report the email.
explanation: Payroll changes involve sensitive data. Use the established HR portal and verify unexpected requests independently.
